rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2-3 and Figures 4-9 report the authors' own development of a 310 g fluorescence LIDAR, its installation on a DJI Matrice 200 quadcopter, and their own field flights over a ~50 m x 100 m maize plot near Semenovskoe (Moscow region) on 24 June, 17 August and 27 September, producing 680/740 nm band-ratio maps.
rows.notes: The study is a technical feasibility demonstration: it shows that a drone-mounted fluorescence LIDAR can map the chlorophyll fluorescence ratio over a maize field during daytime and that spots of altered ratio may indicate plants under stress. It reports no result on crop productivity, yield, resource-use (water, fertilizer, herbicide) efficiency or sustainability outcomes; the statement that fast detection would allow prevention of crop losses is an inference, not a measured result. Detecting/locating stressed plants is only a precondition for the claimed productivity and efficiency gains, so Q2 is no and upstream is set. No ground-truth validation (e.g., lab chlorophyll measurements) was performed; only 10-parallel-measurement reproducibility bands (Figure 5) are shown for the spectra, not for any production effect.

notes: Full text appears complete (short MDPI Communication, 9 pages); some pages are duplicated/garbled in the OCR but all sections are readable. The study is about UAV fluorescence LIDAR, matching the technology in the passage, but reports only sensing feasibility, not the productivity/resource-efficiency effects claimed.
